newsitem.title: USA: Cancer death rate dropping in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Cancer death rate dropping in U.S.

text.p: Cancer death rates have dropped steadily in the 1990s, a trend that public health officials and researchers hailed on Wednesday as a turning point in the war on cancer.
Citing declines in major killers like lung and breast cancers, researchers also predicted a slow but steady decline in the cancer death rate in years to come.

"The 1990s will be remembered as the decade when we measurably turned the tide against cancer," said Dr. Richard Klausner, director of the National Cancer Institute, which released the data along with the American Cancer Society.
Researchers attributed the gains to prevention, early detection and improved treatments.

After rising for decades, the overall cancer mortality rate declined every year from 1990 to 1995, for a total reduction of about 3.1 percent, according to research to be published on Friday in the journal Cancer.

"This is not just a one-time blip but a real and promising downward trend," U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala said in a statement welcoming the report, which was based largely on U.S. government health data.
"This decline is accelerating and is now continuing to about two percent per year," said Dr. Philip Cole, an epidemiologist at the University of Alabama, the lead author of the report in the journal.
Gains have been especially notable in lung, colorectal and prostate cancer in men, and in breast, colorectal and gynecological cancers among women.
And although blacks still have higher cancer disease rates than whites, they have also made bigger gains in reducing mortality -- about 5.6 percent over the five years.
There has been no "magic bullet" against cancer but prevention, early detection and improved treatments have all contributed to the drop in mortality, researchers said.

In an editorial accompanying the journal article, Curtis Mettlin of the Roswell Park Cancer Institute cited anti-smoking campaigns and better breast cancer detection through mammography as key elements in improving survival rates.
In 1990, there were 135 cancer deaths per 100,000 persons. By 1995, the rate had dropped to 131.
Lung cancer deaths dropped 3.9 percent, and other smoking-related cancers dropped 2 percent.
Rates for men in all age groups declined. For women, rates declined under age 65, but rose 2.9 percent for older women.
